case20v1-req.release.metrics:
Chitravel Pay and the Autopay Gate

A decision case on release criteria and success metrics

1. Opening

At 6:10 p.m. on Thursday 15 October 2026, Kiruthika Sundaresan sat in a glass room on the fourth floor of Chitravel Pay's office in Guindy, Chennai, with two documents open. One was the product requirements document for Billmate, a feature that lets a user enrol a recurring bill in UPI AutoPay and be reminded before it falls due. The other was the readout of a fourteen-day pilot.

The last section of the requirements document, written in August, listed six release criteria and one success metric. Two of the six had failed in the pilot. A full rollout was booked for Monday 19 October, and the festive code freeze begins on Monday 26 October. The release review was set for 8:30 p.m. IST on Friday 16 October, which is 11:00 a.m. in Toronto and New Jersey and 11:00 p.m. in Singapore. As head of product she had to tell it what Chitravel Pay would do on Monday.

2. Company background

Chitravel Pay began in 2018 as a bill-payment and recharge app on NPCI's Bharat BillPay network and added UPI payments through a sponsor bank. It now has 1.8 crore registered users, 58 lakh of them active each month, about 640 employees and FY2026 revenue of ₹214 crore, mostly agent fees from billers and merchant payments. PhonePe, Paytm, Google Pay, Amazon Pay and CRED all offer bill payment, so Chitravel Pay competes on reminders in Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam and on a short list of utility billers that people actually pay every month.

Billmate came from support data: late payment was the most common reason users gave when they stopped opening the app. About 21 lakh users have at least one saved recurring biller, and Billmate was built for them. The engineering teams sit in Bengaluru (apps) and Pune (payments platform), and a Dubai remittance partner wants the feature for customers who pay their parents' bills in India.

3. The situation

The pilot ran from Monday 21 September to Sunday 4 October. Kalaivani Sivakumar's team drew two random samples of 40,000 users from the 21 lakh eligible, one offered Billmate and one not. Each user was counted once, on the first bill falling due in the window, so the on-time and ticket rates are over 40,000 users.

The August criteria are in Exhibit 1. The success metric is the on-time rate, meaning the share of eligible users who pay their first due bill on or before the due date, and the target was a gain of 2.0 percentage points over the held-out group by day 28 after launch. The pilot read day 14 (Exhibit 2).

The team sees it differently from each city. Kuberan Sampath in Pune notes that 238 of the 330 failed debits were Bharat BillPay biller timeouts, which he does not count as Chitravel Pay faults, and that a retry-after-two-hours fix needs three weeks. Kalaivani in Toronto reports the gain with its interval and declines to round either end. Kodanda Sadasivan in Singapore has read a sample of the extra tickets and finds many from users surprised by a debit on a date they had chosen weeks earlier. Kranthi Swaminathan in New Jersey has ₹80 lakh of festive media that becomes non-refundable after Wednesday 21 October, shown on the timeline in Figure 1.

4. The people

Kuberan Sampath, engineering manager, Pune. He owns the payments platform and the retry logic. He wants time to fix the timeouts, and he does not want a second incident during Diwali week.

Kalaivani Sivakumar, data scientist, Toronto. She designed the pilot and wants the success metric read as written. She wants a holdout kept after launch, since without one the day-28 target cannot be measured.

Kodanda Sadasivan, customer-success lead, Singapore. His team of 46 answers the tickets at ₹62 each in fully loaded cost. He wants the ticket guardrail respected and the debit reminder rewritten before anyone scales.

Kranthi Swaminathan, head of growth, New Jersey. He wants Billmate live for the festive campaign and for the Dubai partner. He argues the August criteria were set before anyone knew how biller timeouts would behave.

6. The options

Option A: ship to every eligible user on Monday 19 October as planned. This keeps the festive campaign and the Dubai partner on schedule. At pilot rates it spends about ₹96.75 lakh of the ₹1.2 crore cashback budget, adds about ₹7.03 lakh of ticket cost per window, and produces about 17,300 failed debits in the same window (3.58% of 4,83,735 enrolments). It leaves criteria 2 and 3 unmet, and the retry fix is still three weeks away.

Option B: ship in stages, with the August thresholds applied as gates. Billmate goes to 10% on Monday 19 October, 30% on Wednesday 21 October and the rest on Friday 23 October, all ahead of the freeze, but only if criteria 2 and 3 are read again at each step, on the debits and tickets of the preceding 48 hours. It keeps 5% of eligible users (1,05,000) outside the feature as a permanent holdout. It costs Pune engineering attention in the week before the freeze and a review of the two readings at every step, and the first step exposes ₹9.67 lakh of cashback.

Option C: hold until the biller-timeout fix and the reminder rewrite are done. The target date is Monday 16 November. The ₹80 lakh media booking can be pulled without charge if it is cancelled by Wednesday 21 October. It leaves the 80,000 pilot users as they are, spends no further cashback, and misses Dhanteras and Diwali.

7. Questions for discussion

1. What does each of the six readings in Exhibit 1 measure, and over which users or events?

2. Exhibit 2 reports a gain of 2.16 points against a target of 2.0. What does the interval support, and what can it not support?

3. Which of the August criteria gate the release, and which readings should also be tracked after launch?

4. Which option should Kiruthika take on Friday, and which readings after launch would make her change course?

8. A note for the learner

Release criteria answer what must be true to ship; success metrics answer what must be true afterwards. They run on different clocks, and a good requirements document keeps them apart. Here the criteria can be read now, and the success metric cannot be read before about 20 November under Option B (day 28 after the final step), so the decision on Friday turns on how much exposure to buy while the success metric is still unknown.

One defensible path is Option B, taken with discipline. First, read each criterion on its stated base and do not redefine it after the result is known. Removing the 238 biller timeouts would lift debit success to 98.98% (8,884 of 8,976), but the August criterion counted every debit, and the user whose bill failed does not care whose fault it was. Second, treat the shipment as a recorded exception to criteria 2 and 3 at capped exposure, about ₹9.67 lakh of cashback and ₹0.70 lakh of ticket cost at the first step, not as a pass. Third, advance only if the same thresholds hold at 10% and 30%, and stop at 10% if they do not, with Kuberan's retry fix and Kodanda's rewritten reminder as the work that unblocks the next step.

The holdout matters because the pilot interval of 1.49 to 2.83 points spans the 2.0 target, so shipping is not evidence that the target is met. With 1,05,000 held out against about 19.95 lakh treated, the smallest gain detectable is 0.43 points, which is enough to read the target at day 28, around 20 November. Kranthi's campaign can run as booked, with its copy limited to the users who have been reached.
exp40v2-req.release.metrics:
Delivery & Technology · Requirements & Specification · Near-expert depth

Release Criteria and Success Metrics

A release criterion buys information you cannot buy after launch. A success metric buys information you cannot buy before it. The strength of each should be set by how expensive the failure is and how fast it becomes visible — and almost every dysfunction in a launch review comes from a team applying the calibration of one regime to a product living in the other.

1. Two rooms, eleven weeks apart

On Tuesday 18 November 2025, in a meeting room on the second floor of an office off Baner Road in Pune, Meera Kulkarni had a signed firmware image, a regulatory deadline thirteen days away, and a statistical problem she had not expected to have. Meera was vice-president of product at Vartul Grid Systems, which manufactured smart prepaid electricity meters and sold, alongside them, the head-end system that collected readings, pushed configuration and handled the settlement arithmetic. Under a state distribution utility's modernisation programme, Vartul had 2,14,000 of its meters installed and communicating across four circles. Firmware 4.2, ready and code-signed, did two things: it implemented a new net-metering settlement computation that the state electricity regulatory commission had mandated by tariff order to take effect on 1 December, and it tightened the meter's tamper-detection logic, which had nothing to do with the deadline and everything to do with a revenue-protection commitment Vartul had made in its last contract review.

Sandeep Rathore, who ran firmware, had a clean result to show. Firmware 4.2 had gone out over the air to a pilot ring of 4,000 meters in Pune city eleven nights earlier. Zero of them had failed to come back. No bricked modems, no meters stuck in bootloader, no silent stop in reporting. Against a release criterion that read "field failure rate requiring physical intervention must not exceed 1 in 10,000 meters," zero failures in four thousand looked, to almost everyone in the room, like an emphatic pass. Meera did not think it was a pass, and the reason she gave took the meeting past its hour. Zero failures in 4,000 trials does not certify a rate of one in ten thousand. It certifies, at ninety-five percent confidence, a rate no worse than about one in 1,333 — seven and a half times looser than the criterion. And worse, all 4,000 pilot meters carried the same communication module. Vartul's fleet carried three, in a mix of roughly 61, 27 and 12 percent. The pilot had said nothing whatsoever about the other 83,460 meters.

Eleven weeks later, on Thursday 5 February 2026, in a very different room in Gurugram, Rohan Sethi was arguing the opposite case with equal conviction. Rohan was head of product at Vimarsh Support AI, whose agentic support system handled about 3.4 lakh customer conversations a month across 62 client tenants — direct-to-consumer brands, two lending apps, a travel aggregator. The release under discussion would let the agent issue a refund of up to ₹2,000 without routing it to a human approver. Tanvi Iyer, who led the data-science group from Hyderabad, had an offline evaluation on 1,800 human-labelled refund scenarios: six unjustified refunds, a rate of 0.33 percent, against a criterion of 0.5 percent. Tanvi's own view was that the eval set was too small to support the claim — the ninety-five percent upper bound on six failures in 1,800 is about 0.73 percent, comfortably over the line — and that they should label 2,800 more scenarios, at roughly ₹95 each for dual review and adjudication, a spend of about ₹2.66 lakh and three weeks.

Rohan refused. Not because he disagreed with the arithmetic, which was Tanvi's and was correct, but because he thought buying that information offline was the wrong purchase. A wrong refund at Vimarsh cost, on average, ₹840, was visible in a ledger within minutes, and could be stopped by flipping a per-tenant flag. A wrong firmware image at Vartul cost ₹1,150 per truck roll, was invisible until a meter failed to report, and could not be flipped back at all. The two decisions were the same decision in name only. Holding them together — one product manager insisting on more evidence before launch, another insisting on less — is the most useful way to see what release criteria and success metrics actually are, and this page argues that the entire design of both artefacts follows from two properties of the failure they guard: how expensive it is to reverse, and how quickly it announces itself.

2. The idea, and the four camps that disagree about it

Define the terms tightly, because the looseness is where the trouble starts. A release criterion is a proposition about the artefact, evaluable before exposure, whose truth value is a precondition for exposing the artefact to a defined population. It has five parts, and a criterion missing any of them is a slogan: a predicate (what must be true), a measurement procedure (how you will know), a population and sample (on what evidence, of what size, drawn from where), an owner (who is competent to assert it), and a gate class (whether failure blocks, and who may waive it). A success metric is a quantity, defined and instrumented before exposure, measured after it over a stated window against a stated comparison, whose movement is the evidence that the change achieved the outcome it was built for. Its parts are a definition, a window, a comparison — the counterfactual, which is the expensive part — a target, and a pre-committed decision rule saying what the team will do at each range of outcome.

The two artefacts answer questions that are not merely different but are asked of different objects at different times by different people. Release criteria are a proposition about the artefact. Success metrics are a proposition about the world after the artefact. No amount of evidence about the first entails anything about the second. Vartul's firmware could be flawless and the billing-dispute rate could stay exactly where it was, because disputes were driven by consumer mistrust of prepaid metering rather than by settlement arithmetic. Vimarsh's agent could be correct on every refund and still make the business worse, which — as section 8 shows — is close to what happened.

The intellectual lineage runs through two mostly separate traditions that have only recently been forced into the same document. The gate tradition is older and comes from manufacturing and safety engineering: Shewhart's control limits and Deming's insistence that quality is built in rather than inspected in, Juran's fitness-for-use, then the software V-model's exit criteria and the verification-and-validation discipline codified in standards like IEEE 1012 and the quality characteristics of ISO/IEC 25010. Its sharpest commercial expression was Microsoft's ship-room practice of the early 1990s, documented by Cusumano and Selby — the "bug bar" that defined which severities blocked a milestone, the zero-bug-bounce discipline, the named individual who owned the go decision. The metric tradition is younger: Kaplan and Norton's balanced scorecard in 1992 established that a single financial number is a poor controller of an organisation and that it needs counterweights, which is the ancestor of the modern guardrail; Ries's innovation accounting reframed a release as an experiment whose purpose is to generate validated learning; and the online-experimentation literature, best consolidated by Kohavi, Tang and Xu, gave the practice its formal machinery — an overall evaluation criterion, guardrail and degradation metrics, minimum detectable effect, and the statistical hygiene that keeps teams from fooling themselves.

The two traditions collided in the 2000s when continuous delivery made the release itself cheap. Humble and Farley argued that any gate a human checks is a gate that will eventually be skipped under deadline pressure, so the gate must be executable; Google's site-reliability practice went further and made the tolerance explicit as an error budget, converting "do not break things" into "you may break things this much, and when the budget is spent, feature work stops." That single move — from zero tolerance to budgeted tolerance — is the deepest change in the field in thirty years, and it is also the fault line along which practitioners still genuinely disagree.

A continuous-delivery purist and a verification purist will give opposite answers to Meera's question, and both answers are defensible given their premises. The purist verificationist says the criterion was written at one in ten thousand and 4,000 meters cannot demonstrate it, so the release waits. The error-budget practitioner says that the criterion was written as a rate when it should have been written as a budget — a fleet-wide allowance of, say, 120 truck rolls per quarter against which this release draws — and that an absolute rate threshold with no budget context invites exactly the paralysis Vartul had walked into. The point of naming the schools is not to pick one; it is that a product manager refereeing an argument between two competent engineers is usually refereeing an unacknowledged disagreement about which school the product belongs to.

3. Mechanics: what an expert actually writes down

Start with the criterion's anatomy, because the quantitative content lives there. Consider Vartul's criterion as written: "field failure rate requiring physical intervention must not exceed 1 in 10,000 meters." It has a predicate and a threshold. It has no sample size, no confidence level, no statement of which population the sample must represent, and no expiry. Each omission is load-bearing.

Take sample size and confidence first. When a test produces zero failures in n trials, the conventional ninety-five percent upper bound on the underlying rate is approximately 3/n — the so-called rule of three, which falls out of solving (1 − p)n = 0.05. Zero in 4,000 gives 3 ÷ 4,000 = 0.075 percent, or 7.5 per 10,000. To certify a rate of 1 per 10,000 with zero observed failures, a team needs n ≥ 3 ÷ 0.0001 = 30,000 meters. At Vartul's over-the-air throughput of about 18,000 meters per night in the utility's maintenance window, plus a mandatory seven-day soak before reading results, that is a nine-day programme — which, on 18 November, ends on 27 November, three days before the regulator's date, with no margin for a failure that would restart the clock.

The two shaded facts a team must internalise are that a point estimate and a bound are different claims, and that the sample size required to certify a rare event grows inversely with the rate you are trying to certify, not with the size of the population you intend to expose. Vimarsh's row is the instructive one: 0.33 percent observed against a 0.5 percent criterion looks like a fifty-percent margin and is in fact a coin flip, because at n = 1,800 the interval is wider than the margin. Going from 1,800 to 4,600 labelled scenarios buys you the right to make the claim you already thought you were making. Whether that right is worth ₹2.66 lakh and three weeks is a business question, not a statistical one — and it is exactly the business question Rohan answered "no" to.

Representativeness dominates sample size

The deeper problem in Meera's room was not that 4,000 was too small. It was that 4,000 was drawn from one stratum. Firmware does not fail at random; it fails deterministically on a configuration class. A modem driver that mishandles a particular baseband firmware revision will brick every meter carrying that module and none of the others. Under that model, the relevant question is not "what is the fleet failure rate" but "have I sampled every configuration in which a distinct failure mechanism could hide." Vartul's fleet split 1,30,540 meters on module vendor A, 57,780 on B, and 25,680 on C. A class-wide defect in the C population would brick 25,680 meters at ₹1,150 a visit — ₹2.95 crore, against a project whose entire annual margin on this contract was smaller than that.

The correct reformulation is a shift from estimation to detection. Instead of "the rate must be below p," write "the ring must have at least a ninety-five percent probability of surfacing any defect mode affecting 0.25 percent or more of any configuration stratum." The sample size follows from 1 − (1 − 0.0025)n ≥ 0.95, which gives n ≥ ln(0.05) ÷ ln(0.9975) ≈ 1,197 — call it 1,200 per stratum, 3,600 meters in total, two nights of over-the-air capacity rather than two weeks. The stratified ring is weaker as an estimator (each stratum's rule-of-three bound is only 0.25 percent) and far stronger as a detector, which is what a pre-release cohort is actually for. Sandeep's team could have it soaking by Thursday.

The success-metric side has its own arithmetic

Success metrics require three numbers written before launch that teams routinely write after. The first is the minimum effect worth detecting. If Vartul's billing-dispute rate among net-metered consumers is 41 per 1,000 per cycle and the project's business case assumed a fall to 12, the team is claiming a 71 percent relative reduction — an enormous effect that would be visible in a few hundred accounts. If the business case had claimed 41 to 37, a ten percent relative move, detecting it reliably at conventional power on a proportion that size needs several thousand accounts per arm, which Vartul's 9,300 net-metered consumers barely supply once you split them. Writing the target before checking whether the sample can support it is how teams arrive, ninety days later, at a result that is neither a win nor a loss and cannot be made into either.

The second number is the window, which must exceed the latency of the mechanism you are measuring. Billing disputes arise on a monthly settlement cycle; a fourteen-day read measures nothing but the tail of the previous cycle. Supply-side churn on a marketplace, as Vichitra Bazaar found out, has a latency closer to ninety days, because a disappointed seller does not resign, they simply stop restocking. The third number is the comparison. Without a holdback — a cohort deliberately denied the feature — a post-launch metric measures the feature plus the season plus the marketing calendar plus whatever else moved. Holdbacks are unpopular because they feel like deliberately withholding value, and they are the single highest-yield discipline in the entire practice.

Second-order effects the mechanics create

Three consequences follow from doing this properly, and all three are usually left implicit. First, tightening a release criterion transfers cost from the post-launch budget to the pre-launch calendar, and because calendar is the scarcer resource in most organisations, a very strict criteria list quietly produces larger, rarer, riskier releases — the opposite of what its authors intended. Second, a criterion that is easy to measure crowds out one that is hard to measure, so criteria lists drift toward the instrumentable and away from the important; the drift is invisible because every individual criterion looks reasonable. Third, publishing a success metric changes the behaviour of the people whose work it measures, which is Goodhart's law operating on your own team rather than on your users — the guardrail exists precisely because the north star will be gamed, not because anyone on the team is dishonest.

4. When the idea applies, and when it actively misleads

The conditions can be stated as four testable claims. Applied to the two protagonists they give, in three of four cases, opposite answers — which is the strongest available evidence that release criteria are not a universal practice but a calibrated one.

Claim one: reversal is cheap. If the change can be withdrawn in minutes at negligible cost, the value of pre-launch evidence collapses, because production is a cheaper and better-powered test than any staging environment. True for Vimarsh, where a per-tenant flag reverts the agent to human approval in under a minute and the residual cost is whatever refunds already went out. Emphatically false for Vartul: an over-the-air firmware push to a meter that no longer boots cannot be recalled, and the recovery is a technician on a two-wheeler.

Claim two: failure is fast and unambiguously visible. Vimarsh's unjustified refunds appear in a settlement ledger within the hour, and a human audit of the first 500 auto-approved refunds gives a direct read. Vartul's failure mode is silence — a meter that stops reporting looks, for up to 48 hours, exactly like a congested mesh, which is why the utility's own outage dashboards would not have flagged it and why the soak period is seven days rather than one.

Claim three: exposure is controllable at a fine grain. Vimarsh can expose four tenants of 62, cap individual refunds at ₹2,000 and daily tenant spend at ₹40,000, which bounds the worst monthly loss across the pilot at about ₹48 lakh in theory and, at a 0.73 percent worst-case error rate on roughly 22,000 monthly refund conversations at an average ₹840, at about ₹1.35 lakh in practice. Vartul can stage by ring but cannot stage by feature, because the firmware image is signed and type-approved as a single blob; splitting the net-metering change from the tamper change would require re-certification at a designated test laboratory, a six-to-eight-week path that makes the December date impossible.

Claim four: pre-launch measurement predicts post-launch behaviour. This is the construct-validity question and it is where AI products break. Vimarsh's 1,800-scenario eval set was assembled in October against a model version that the provider replaced in January. An eval set is a photograph of a distribution, and both the model and the traffic move underneath it. Vartul's position is better: a meter in a lab responds to a firmware image in the same way a meter in Baramati does, provided the configuration matches — which is precisely why stratification, not sample size, was the binding constraint.

The idea becomes actively misleading in two situations. The first is when the criteria list becomes the operational definition of quality, at which point engineers optimise against the list and the residual risk migrates to everything the list does not mention; the tell is a release that passes every criterion and generates a support incident nobody had a name for. The second is when the cost of delay is real and uncounted. Waiting is not free and not neutral: at Vartul, missing the regulator's date meant the utility settling 9,300 solar accounts by hand, and a team that computes the cost of shipping wrong but refuses to compute the cost of shipping late is not being rigorous, it is being one-sided in a way that always resolves in the same direction.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Four situations break the clean picture, and in each the interesting failure is organisational rather than technical.

Regulated hardware with software inside. Vartul's inability to split a signed firmware image is not an engineering limitation; it is a certification artefact. Type approval attaches to the image, so any feature-level decomposition — the obvious product-management move of shipping the deadline-bound change and holding the risky one — requires re-testing at a designated laboratory. The practical consequence is that in certified hardware, release criteria are coarser than product managers want and the only available dial is population, not scope. Mature firms respond by architecting for the dial they do have: feature flags inside the certified image, so that behaviour can be enabled per-meter by configuration push rather than by firmware push, with the flag-off path being the certified default. Vartul had built exactly such a mechanism for two earlier features and had not, on this release, extended it to net metering — a decision made eight months earlier by an engineer optimising for image size that turned into Meera's constraint in November. This is the most common shape of an edge case: a release problem that is really an architecture decision arriving late.

Two-sided markets. A marketplace has at least two populations whose metrics can move in opposite directions, and a release-criteria list that tests only the transacting path will pass a change that is fatal to the supply side. The structural trap is that demand-side effects are fast and supply-side effects are slow, so a thirty-day read systematically over-weights the buyer and under-weights the seller. Section 8 works the numbers on Vichitra Bazaar, where exactly this happened.

AI-native products. Three properties break the standard machinery. Output is non-deterministic, so a criterion must specify at which quantile of repeated runs it holds — Vimarsh ran each eval scenario three times and scored the worst of the three, which is a defensible but unusually strict choice that Tanvi argued for and which itself cost them roughly a third of their apparent pass rate. The evaluation set decays, because model providers ship new versions on their own calendar; Vimarsh's October eval set was, by February, a measurement of a system that no longer existed, and the honest move is to date every eval result and treat it as expiring. And the failure distribution is long-tailed in a way that sampling handles badly: the six unjustified refunds in Tanvi's set were all in one semantic neighbourhood — customers who claimed non-delivery on orders marked delivered — which means the true risk was not a 0.33 percent random rate but a near-certainty on a specific scenario class that happened to be rare in the sample. The expert response is to stratify evals the way Vartul stratified its meter ring: by failure mechanism, not by volume.

Multi-product platforms and the seam problem. When five teams ship on one release train, criteria ownership fragments. The platform team owns the non-functional criteria, each feature team owns its functional ones, a central quality function owns the process, and nobody owns the interaction. In practice mature companies manage this with a device they rarely describe in public: a waiver ledger. Every criterion that was not met but was shipped anyway is recorded with the name of the person who accepted the residual risk, the reason, and an expiry date by which it must be cleared. What organisations say is that their criteria are gates. What they do is run a waiver ledger, and the health of a release process is legible far more from the ledger than from the criteria document — a ledger with forty open waivers, twelve of them expired, describes an organisation whose gates are decorative, and it describes it far more honestly than any dashboard.

6. Ten distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A threshold without a sample size and a confidence level is not a criterion. The tell-tale sign is a criteria document where every row is a number and a comparison operator and no row has an n. The obvious reading — that specifying the threshold is the hard part and the measurement is a detail — is backwards: a threshold is easy to agree and impossible to falsify without the measurement plan, which is why criteria written this way are the ones that get argued about in the go/no-go meeting. An expert reads a criteria list by looking first at the evidence column, and if the evidence column does not exist, concludes that the list has never actually blocked anything.

A pilot cohort is a detector, not an estimator, and should be sized for power against a named failure mechanism. The tell is a pilot population chosen by convenience — the friendliest customer, the nearest circle, the internal dogfood group. Convenience samples have systematically lower variance than the fleet on exactly the dimensions that matter, because the friendliest customer has the newest hardware and the most patient staff. The obvious reading, that a bigger pilot is a better pilot, is wrong in the case that matters: 3,600 stratified meters told Vartul more than 4,000 homogeneous ones, at ninety percent of the cost.

Criteria decay, and evidence has an as-of date. A test that passed six weeks ago is a claim about a system that has since taken forty commits, a dependency bump and a model-provider update. The tell is a release-readiness document where results have no timestamps. Experts date every row and set an expiry proportional to the rate of change of the thing measured — a static compliance check might hold for a quarter, an AI eval for a fortnight, a performance benchmark until the next dependency change. The obvious reading is that re-running everything is wasteful; the correct reading is that the expensive waste is a launch decision made on stale evidence nobody realised was stale.

The waiver ledger is the real policy document. The tell is that no such ledger exists, which does not mean waivers do not happen — it means they happen verbally and are never revisited. Experts ask to see the last four releases' waivers before they read the current criteria list, because the waivers reveal which criteria the organisation actually treats as binding. The obvious reading, that waivers indicate weak discipline, inverts the truth: a well-run process has waivers, recorded, owned and expiring; a process with none has either trivially weak criteria or unrecorded exceptions.

The north star usually measures the mechanism, not the outcome. "Percentage of refunds handled without a human" is a measure of whether the feature ran, not of whether the business got better. The tell is a north star that cannot go down for any reason other than the feature being switched off. Experts insist the north star be expressed in a unit the finance function recognises — cost per resolved issue, disputes per thousand consumers, contribution per active seller — because mechanism metrics always move on launch and therefore contain no information. The obvious reading is that a metric which reliably moves is a good metric; the opposite is true, and a metric that only ever moves one way is a progress bar wearing a metric's clothing.

Guardrails must be read as trends, not levels, over a window longer than the mechanism's latency. The tell is a launch review that reports single day-30 numbers with no time series. Vimarsh's repeat-contact rate was 13.4 percent at the day-21 read against an 8.1 percent baseline; the number that mattered was not 13.4 but the sequence 9.2, 11.6, 13.4, 14.1, which was still climbing. The obvious reading — that a guardrail either breached or did not — discards the only part of the data that forecasts. Experts set guardrail thresholds on the second derivative as often as on the level.

The counterfactual is the expensive part, and pre-post comparison is almost always wrong. The tell is the phrase "compared to last month" in a launch review. Seasonality, marketing spend, a competitor's outage and the festive calendar all move the same numbers. Experts negotiate a holdback cohort before launch, when it costs an argument, rather than after, when it costs the entire read. The obvious objection — that holdbacks deny value to real customers — is correct and is the price of knowing anything; the useful counter is that a holdback of five percent for six weeks costs less than one quarter of building the wrong next feature.

Pre-register the decomposition, not just the metric. The tell is a post-launch review that spends most of its time arguing about which slice to look at. If the metric is flat overall, someone will find a cohort where it moved, and that cohort will be believed. Experts name, before launch, the three cuts that will be examined and commit to reading all three regardless of what they show. The obvious reading is that exploring the data afterwards is good analytical practice; it is good exploratory practice and terrible confirmatory practice, and launch reviews are confirmatory.

Repeated peeking at a live metric guarantees an eventual false alarm. A guardrail checked daily against a fixed threshold will breach by chance sooner or later; over thirty independent daily checks at a nominal five percent level, the probability of at least one spurious breach is 1 − 0.9530 ≈ 79 percent. The tell is a team that has learned to ignore its own alerts. The obvious reading — that the threshold should be loosened — treats the symptom; the correct treatment is a sequential procedure with an explicit alpha-spending schedule, or a much simpler rule that a breach must persist for two consecutive reads before it counts.

The cost of delay is a number, and refusing to compute it is not conservatism. The tell is a launch discussion where every risk is quantified and waiting is treated as the costless default. At Vartul, delay had a price: a manual settlement run for 9,300 solar accounts, costed by the utility's commercial team at three person-weeks and about ₹6.8 lakh of temporary staffing, plus a written intimation to the commission. That number, once on the table, changed the shape of the conversation entirely — not because ₹6.8 lakh is large but because it converted an argument about principle into an argument about price, which is the kind an organisation can actually settle. The obvious reading, that quantifying delay pressures teams into shipping unsafely, gets it backwards: unquantified delay costs are exactly what lets the loudest deadline win.

7. How the practice differs by product type and company stage

The differences are real in some places and imaginary in others, and it is worth saying plainly which is which. The genuine variation is almost entirely explained by the two axes of the diagram in section 4 — reversibility and detection latency — plus a third that only appears in enterprise and regulated settings, which is whether the gate's authority is internal or external.

An early-stage company does not have a different theory of release criteria; it has a different sample size and therefore a different achievable confidence, and its honest response is to write criteria it can actually evaluate and to substitute qualitative evidence — eight customer calls rather than a proportion test — while being explicit that it is accepting a much higher probability of being fooled in exchange for speed. The failure mode of early-stage teams is not that they skip criteria; it is that they import a large company's criteria template and then waive nine-tenths of it, which trains the team to treat the whole document as theatre. The failure mode of large companies is the mirror image: criteria accumulate because every past incident adds a row and nothing is ever removed, until the pre-launch checklist takes three weeks and the organisation responds by batching releases, which raises risk. A useful discipline, rare in practice, is to sunset criteria — every row is reviewed annually and must justify itself by having blocked something or by guarding a risk that still exists.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Vartul: buying the right evidence rather than more of it

Meera's team re-cut the problem in two working days. The original criterion — a rate of 1 in 10,000 — was replaced by a detection criterion: ninety-five percent probability of surfacing any defect mode affecting 0.25 percent or more of any module-vendor stratum, which required 1,200 meters per stratum, 3,600 in total, one night of over-the-air capacity and a seven-day soak. Against the alternative of 30,000 homogeneous meters and a nine-day programme, the stratified ring cost less calendar and covered the ₹2.95 crore exposure that the original pilot had entirely missed. The residual risk was explicit and written down: a defect affecting fewer than 0.25 percent of a stratum could still escape, with an expected worst case of 0.0025 × 25,680 = 64 vendor-C meters, or about ₹74,000 in truck rolls — a number small enough to accept, and, importantly, a number nobody had computed under the original criterion because the original criterion had no failure model at all.

Vimarsh: the north star that measured the wrong thing

Rohan shipped on 9 February to four tenants with a ₹2,000 per-refund cap, a ₹40,000 daily tenant budget, and a standing human audit of every auto-approved refund for the first 500 cases. The release criteria he actually gated on were three: that the circuit breaker reverted to human approval within sixty seconds of a manual trigger, that the daily budget cap was enforced server-side rather than in the agent's prompt, and that every auto-approved refund wrote an immutable audit record with the evidence the agent relied on. Note what those three have in common — none of them is about whether the model is right. They are all about whether being wrong is survivable. That is the correct criteria list for the bottom-right quadrant.

The success metrics were where it got interesting. The north star, chosen in January, was automation rate: the share of refund conversations resolved without a human. It went from zero to 71 percent in three weeks and everyone was delighted. The guardrail, chosen almost as an afterthought by Tanvi, was seven-day repeat-contact rate among auto-refunded customers, baselined at 8.1 percent. It went 9.2, 11.6, 13.4 and was still climbing at week four. The mechanism was mundane and would have been invisible without the guardrail: the agent refunded correctly and then closed the conversation, without fixing the underlying problem — a wrong item shipped, an address on file that was stale — so the customer came back a few days later with the same complaint and a worse mood.

The corrective was to redefine the north star as cost per resolved issue, where a repeat contact counts against the same issue rather than opening a new one, which mechanically forces the metric to absorb the failure the old one hid.

Vichitra Bazaar: the failure, and what recovery actually cost

Vichitra Bazaar, a Jaipur-based marketplace connecting handicraft artisans with domestic buyers, shipped a verified-artisan badge and an accompanying ranking change in the first week of a financial year. Its release criteria were exemplary by the standards of the consumer school: crash-free session rate above 99.6 percent, search latency under 400 milliseconds at the ninety-fifth percentile, badge issuance reconciled against the verification queue with zero discrepancies, and a staged exposure at 10, 50 and 100 percent of buyers over nine days. Every criterion passed. The north star, gross merchandise value, was up 14.2 percent against a five percent holdback at the thirty-day read — a clean, well-instrumented, statistically respectable win, and the team said so in a launch review that lasted twenty minutes.

The guardrail they had chosen was seller-side order fulfilment rate, which stayed flat at 96 percent. The guardrail they had not chosen was the distribution of demand across sellers. Ranking now favoured verified artisans, and verification required a GST registration and a bank account in the business's name, which about 38 percent of Vichitra's 11,000 active artisans did not have. The share of GMV flowing to sellers with fewer than fifty lifetime orders fell from 31 percent to 12 percent in six weeks. Nothing about that breached any threshold, because no threshold existed for it.

The consequence arrived on the supply side's own clock. Unverified artisans did not complain or churn in any way a dashboard registers; they simply stopped restocking. By day 90, roughly 2,400 artisans had gone dormant and listing breadth — distinct active SKUs — was down 19 percent. By day 150, GMV was 6 percent below the pre-launch baseline, because buyers arriving for the long tail of unusual pieces were finding a thinner catalogue and converting worse. The recovery took two quarters and about ₹3.2 crore in seller re-acquisition incentives and verification assistance camps run in six craft clusters, and it did not fully restore listing breadth.

What the team changed afterwards is the instructive part, and it was not a change to their release criteria, which had been fine. They changed three things about metrics. They added supply-side concentration — the share of GMV going to the bottom two quartiles of sellers by order history — as a hard guardrail with a threshold of no more than a four-point fall. They split the read window: a thirty-day read on buyer-side metrics and a ninety-day read on seller-side metrics, with an explicit rule that the launch could not be declared successful until both had reported. And they introduced a supply-side holdback — a cohort of sellers whose ranking treatment was unchanged — which is operationally awkward on a marketplace and was the only way to separate the ranking effect from the ordinary seasonal churn of a craft business. The cost of catching this late was not the ₹3.2 crore; it was that for five months the organisation believed a false thing about its own product and made three roadmap decisions on the strength of it.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings, and the cost of a late catch

The failure modes below recur across company types with remarkable consistency. What varies is only how expensive each becomes when caught late, and the variation tracks the reversibility axis exactly.

Unrecorded waivers look like pragmatism and trust; what they actually do is convert a written policy into an oral tradition, and oral traditions drift in the direction of whoever speaks last before a deadline. And daily guardrail checking looks like vigilance; what it produces is an organisation that has trained itself to ignore its own instruments, which is strictly worse than having no instruments, because the false confidence is now institutionalised.

10. Where competent experts genuinely disagree

Four disagreements in this field are live, and none of them is resolved by a synthesis that anyone actually holds.

Should the ship decision be a meeting or a pipeline? The automation position, steelmanned, rests on strong evidence: the DORA research programme's consistent finding that elite performers deploy far more frequently with lower change-failure rates, and the mechanism is understood — small batches localise causes, and a gate a machine evaluates cannot be talked out of. Its adherents argue that a go/no-go meeting is an admission that the team cannot articulate its criteria precisely enough to execute them. The human-judgement position, equally steelmanned, observes that the most consequential release risks are the ones nobody wrote a check for — a change that is technically correct and commercially catastrophic, a launch landing in the same week as a regulatory filing — and that these are pattern-matched by an experienced person in a room and by nothing else. What would have to be true for the automation school to be wrong: that the residual, unautomatable risks carry more expected loss than the batch-size and consistency gains, which is plausibly true exactly in Vartul's quadrant and implausible in Vimarsh's.

Should success metrics ever gate anything? The kill-criteria school holds that a team should pre-commit, before launch, to a metric threshold below which the feature is removed — otherwise every feature survives, the product accretes, and the organisation never learns. Its evidence is the observable fact that features are almost never removed, and that post-hoc rationalisation of a flat result is nearly universal. The opposing school argues that pre-committed kill thresholds are set in ignorance of what the team will learn, that many valuable features are slow, and that a hard kill rule mostly succeeds in teaching people to set unambitious targets they can clear. What would have to be true for the kill-criteria school to be right: that the cost of carrying dead features exceeds the option value of slow-burning ones — which is an empirical question with a different answer in a two-year-old product than in a twelve-year-old one.

One north star, or a scorecard? The single-metric school argues that a lone number forces prioritisation and makes trade-offs explicit, and points to the coordination benefits in large organisations where a scorecard becomes a menu from which each team selects the metric it happens to have moved. The scorecard school invokes Goodhart directly: any single metric will be optimised into uselessness, and the balanced-scorecard tradition exists precisely because that is what happened to single financial measures. The interesting thing is that both sides now largely agree on the practical arrangement — one north star with a small, fixed, non-negotiable set of guardrails — while continuing to disagree about whether the guardrails are subordinate to the north star or co-equal with it, which matters enormously the day they conflict. Vimarsh's case is exactly that day, and the answer the team gave — redefine the north star to absorb the guardrail — is one defensible resolution among several.

Is an offline evaluation a legitimate release criterion for an AI product at all? The affirmative position holds that an eval set is the only pre-exposure evidence available and that abandoning it means shipping with no gate whatsoever; its evidence is the class of catastrophic errors — unsafe advice, systematic bias against a customer segment — that must never reach a user even once, and for which a post-hoc metric is no comfort. The sceptical position, which Rohan held, is that offline evals measure a distribution that is not production's, decay silently as models change, and generate false confidence disproportionate to their power, so the honest gate is containment — caps, audits, reversibility — and the honest measurement happens in production under observation. What would have to be true for the sceptics to be wrong: that some failure modes are both severe enough that a single occurrence is unacceptable and detectable offline. That is straightforwardly true for a medical or legal advice product and straightforwardly false for a ₹2,000 refund, which is why the disagreement persists — both camps are generalising correctly from different products.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes better documents. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently, and the difference is visible within one meeting.

They ask about reversibility and detection latency before they ask about anything else, because those two properties determine the entire shape of the answer, and a practitioner who begins by drafting criteria has already skipped the decision that matters. They write criteria that can fail — and can tell you the last time one did, which is the single best test of whether a gate is real. They treat the measurement plan as the substance of the criterion and the threshold as the easy part, so their documents have an evidence column with dates and sample sizes, and their pilot cohorts are stratified by failure mechanism rather than assembled by convenience. And they hold the two artefacts apart with something close to stubbornness: when an anxious executive in a go/no-go meeting raises an objection about whether the feature will work, they name it as a metrics question, put a date on the calendar when it will be answered, and return the room to the question of whether the gate is honestly passed. That last move looks like process pedantry and is in fact the most valuable thing a product manager does in a launch review, because it is the only thing that prevents a launch decision from being made on evidence that does not yet exist.

The negative version is equally diagnostic. Someone with genuine command of this will tell you when the practice does not apply — will say, of a two-person team shipping to forty users, that the correct release criterion is "it does not lose data" and the correct success metric is "eight customers tell us what happened," and will resist the pull toward a formality the situation cannot support. The discipline is not a checklist. It is a way of pricing information: what is it worth to know this before we expose it, and what will it cost to find out after?

12. The decisions, and three questions

Meera did not ship the full fleet, did not run the 30,000-meter programme, and did not miss the regulator's date. She authorised the stratified ring — 1,200 meters on each of the three module vendors, pushed over two nights beginning 20 November, with a seven-day soak — and simultaneously asked the utility's commercial team to prepare a manual settlement fallback for the 9,300 net-metered accounts at a cost of ₹6.8 lakh, with a written intimation to the commission that settlement for the December cycle would be performed manually pending firmware validation. The second move is the one worth studying: she converted an externally-owned hard gate into an internally-owned soft one by buying a process fallback, which is almost always cheaper than it looks and almost never considered. The ring surfaced two failures, both on vendor B, both traced to a modem power-management interaction; the fix took four days; the fleet rollout began on 8 December and completed without a truck roll. In her own account of it afterwards, the decision she was proudest of was not the ring but rewriting the criterion from a rate to a detection power, because the rate version had been unmeetable and therefore, in practice, waivable.

Rohan shipped on 9 February to four tenants with the circuit breaker, the ₹2,000 cap and the 500-refund human audit, and never bought the additional 2,800 labelled scenarios. He was right about the containment and wrong about the measurement: the north star he had chosen in January was a mechanism metric, and only Tanvi's afterthought guardrail caught what was happening. The rollout to the remaining 58 tenants was held until the north star had been redefined as cost per resolved issue and re-baselined, which cost six weeks — six weeks Rohan had been unwilling to spend on evals and was willing to spend on measurement, which is a coherent position and an uncomfortable one to defend in a room that remembers the earlier argument.

Three questions for discussion.

1. Meera's team met the regulator's date by buying a manual process fallback for ₹6.8 lakh rather than by shipping software. If that option had been available and unexamined for three years — as it had been — what does that say about how Vartul's product organisation framed its constraints, and what is the equivalent unexamined fallback in a product you work on?

2. Rohan refused ₹2.66 lakh of pre-launch evidence and then spent six weeks of post-launch delay on re-measurement. Was that a good trade, a bad trade, or the same trade priced in a currency he preferred? What would have had to be true about the refund cap for the answer to change?

3. Vichitra Bazaar's release criteria were, by consumer-product standards, exemplary, and its launch was still a failure. If no release criterion could have caught it, where should the accountability for that outcome sit — with the criteria, with the metric design, or with whoever decided a thirty-day window was long enough for a marketplace?

13. Going deeper

PRD structure. Release criteria are the closing section of a PRD and the one that most often goes unwritten; seeing where they sit in the document explains why they end up vague, and writing them in the PRD rather than in the launch week is the single highest-leverage change most teams can make.

Building a metrics dashboard. A success metric that cannot be instrumented reliably before launch is not a metric a team will respect at day thirty; the dashboard work is where definitions get forced into precision and where the cuts you pre-registered either exist or do not.

Release management and launch readiness. The organisational machinery — rings, rollback plans, on-call rotations, waiver ledgers — that turns a passed criteria list into a launch that survives contact with reality. It is the layer directly above this one and the natural next stop.

PM artefacts: one-pager, PRD, spec, strategy doc. Knowing which artefact carries which commitment prevents the specific failure this page opened with — a gate condition and an outcome target living in the same document under the same heading.

Writing a one-pager. The place where the success metric is first proposed, usually before anyone has checked whether the available sample can detect the claimed effect; getting the minimum detectable effect into the one-pager saves a quarter later.

Customer narratives (Day 0 / Day N). The Day N narrative is where guardrail metrics come from, because it is the only artefact that forces a team to describe what the customer's life looks like after the novelty wears off — which is precisely the window Vichitra Bazaar failed to examine.

Acceptance criteria and error cases. Story-level acceptance criteria and release-level criteria are different instruments at different grains; conflating them produces release gates made of a hundred unit assertions and no statement about the system.

Telemetry requirements. Every guardrail in this page presupposes an event that someone specified before the code was written. Telemetry written after launch is telemetry that measures what was easy to capture rather than what you needed to know.

Non-functional requirements. Latency, availability, capacity and privacy obligations supply most of the non-functional rows in any criteria list, and the error-budget framing that makes them tractable rather than absolute lives in that topic.

Release Criteria and Success Metrics

What has to be true before a team is allowed to ship, and what has to be true afterwards for the shipping to have been worth it — and why conflating the two is the single most expensive habit in a launch review.

A Thursday in March, Chandigarh

Priya Raman had booked the launch review for forty-five minutes, and by minute thirty she knew it was going to run long. Priya was vice-president of product at Jagriti Health Cloud, a Chandigarh-based company that sold appointment, billing and records software to roughly nine hundred small and mid-sized clinics across north India. The feature under review was Smart Intake, an assistant that used a language model to read a patient's spoken or typed complaint at the front desk and suggest which department they should be routed to — general medicine, orthopaedics, gynaecology, and so on — before a human receptionist confirmed or overrode it. The company's engineering lead, Arvind Suri, had a build ready. The question on the table, the only question that mattered, was whether Jagriti should ship it to its first twenty pilot clinics on April 6, nine days away.

Priya had two documents open. One was a checklist Arvind's team had assembled: test results, latency numbers, a data-privacy sign-off. The other was a slide Priya herself had built two months earlier, titled "Why Smart Intake Matters," which promised that the feature would cut the average time from patient walk-in to being seen by the right department from just over fourteen minutes to under ten. Somewhere in the room, without anyone quite naming it, the two documents had gotten tangled together. Arvind's checklist was being treated as proof that the feature would work. Priya's slide was being treated as a condition for shipping — as though April 6 should be delayed until someone could guarantee the ten-minute number. Neither was correct, and the confusion was about to cost Jagriti a week it did not have, because the clinics' billing-software renewal cycle closed at the end of the month and a slipped launch meant missing the sales team's entire pitch window for a fifth of the client base.

What Priya needed, and did not yet have on paper, was two separate and differently shaped things: a set of release criteria — binary, checkable conditions that had to be true on April 6 itself, before a single patient's routing decision was trusted to the model — and a set of success metrics — measurements that could only be taken after real clinics had used the thing for weeks, that would tell Jagriti whether the fourteen-to-ten-minute bet had paid off. Getting this distinction straight, and getting the two documents built correctly, is the subject of this page.

The idea, defined plainly

Release criteria are the finite list of conditions that must be verifiably true about a product before it is allowed in front of real users, or in front of more of them. They are a gate, not a forecast. A release criterion does not predict that the feature will succeed; it certifies that the feature is safe and functional enough that finding out whether it succeeds is a reasonable risk to take. Success metrics are the measurements, defined and instrumented before launch, that will be read afterward to judge whether the product achieved the outcome it was built for. They are a scoreboard, not a gate. A team can pass every release criterion and still fail every success metric — the feature can work exactly as specified and still not move the needle it was meant to move. The reverse can also happen, less often: a rough, incompletely-tested release can occasionally still produce a metric win, which is precisely why criteria and metrics have to be evaluated separately rather than treated as two readings of the same instrument.

The vocabulary crystallised out of software engineering practice from the 1990s onward, as teams shipping in tight cycles needed a formal answer to "are we done" that did not depend on any one engineer's gut feel; release-readiness checklists and "exit criteria" show up in IEEE and ISO software-quality standards from roughly that period, and the discipline was sharpened further by the DevOps and continuous-delivery movement of the 2000s, which forced teams to make release criteria automatable rather than a matter of a manager's judgment call the night before. Success metrics, as a formal companion practice, matured alongside product analytics tooling in the 2010s — the point at which "ship it and see" became "ship it, measure it against a number we wrote down in advance, and be honest about what we find." The sentence Priya could say in that room without sounding glib is this: release criteria answer whether we are allowed to find out; success metrics answer whether it was worth finding out.

The mechanics, walked through with Smart Intake

Building a release-criteria list starts with a step teams routinely skip: sorting candidate criteria into categories, because a criterion that belongs to one category is judged differently from a criterion that belongs to another, and mixing them produces exactly the muddle Priya was sitting in. The categories that mattered for Smart Intake were four. Functional criteria ask whether the feature does the specific thing it claims to do — here, whether the routing suggestion was clinically reasonable often enough to trust. Non-functional criteria ask whether it does that thing fast enough, reliably enough, and at a scale the business needs — response latency, uptime, behaviour under a receptionist typing two complaints in ten seconds. Compliance and safety criteria ask whether the feature is legally and ethically permitted to exist in its current form — for a health product handling patient complaints, this meant conformance with India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and a redaction check ensuring no patient-identifying text left Jagriti's systems unencrypted. Operational-readiness criteria ask whether the organisation around the feature, not just the feature itself, is prepared — a rollback plan, an on-call rota, a support script for receptionists who hit an error.

The second step, the one Arvind's team had done well, is turning each category into specific, measurable thresholds rather than adjectives. "Fast" is not a criterion; "P95 response latency under 2.5 seconds, measured under a simulated load of forty concurrent front desks" is one. The third step, which the Jagriti team had not yet done, is deciding in advance which criteria are hard gates — any failure blocks the release, no exceptions — and which are soft, negotiable in a documented trade-off conversation between product and engineering leadership. Compliance criteria are almost always hard gates. Some non-functional criteria can be soft, if a team is explicit that it is accepting a known, bounded risk. The fourth step is building the success-metrics side in parallel, not afterward: naming one north-star metric that the feature is being built to move, naming two or three guardrail metrics that must not get worse even if the north star improves, and writing down, before launch, the exact definition, the measurement window, and the target for each — because a metric defined after the data comes in is not a metric, it is a story.

The go/no-go review, worked line by line

Arvind's team had run Smart Intake's routing suggestion against five hundred real, anonymised historical intake records, scored by two senior nurses as "correct," "acceptable," or "wrong" department. The functional release criterion Priya had approved eight weeks earlier read: at least 95% of routing suggestions must be scored "correct" against the two-nurse panel, on a held-out sample of at least 500 cases. The result that came back was 471 cases marked strictly "correct" out of 500. That is 471 ÷ 500 = 0.942, or 94.2%. Against a 95% hard gate, Smart Intake failed by 0.8 percentage points — not a rounding error, and under the criterion as written, not shippable on April 6.

This is where launch reviews usually go one of two bad ways: someone argues the number is "close enough," which quietly turns a hard gate into a soft one without anyone deciding that on purpose, or someone insists on a full re-training cycle that blows the April 6 date. Priya did neither. She asked Arvind's team to break the 29 "wrong" cases down by what the nurses meant by wrong. Eighteen of the 29 were cases where Smart Intake's suggested department was "acceptable" under the panel's own three-way scale — a borderline call, not a dangerous one, such as suggesting general medicine instead of ENT for a patient describing a sore throat with fever. Eleven were genuine misroutes, including two that sent a chest-pain complaint to a non-urgent queue, which is the exact failure mode the criterion existed to catch.

Running the arithmetic a second way, counting "correct" and "acceptable" together against the panel's own definitions, gives 471 + 18 = 489 out of 500, or 97.8%. That number comfortably clears 95% — but it answers a different, looser question than the one the criterion was written to ask, and Priya's job in the room was to notice that difference rather than let whichever number was more convenient quietly become the official one. Her actual decision, discussed in the closing section below, treated the eleven genuine misroutes — 11 ÷ 500 = 2.2% — as the number that mattered, and asked a narrower, cheaper question: could that 2.2% be brought down without a full re-train.

Eight distinctions a careful reader should hold onto

A criterion is not a metric wearing a deadline

The most common error, and the one Priya's team nearly made, is writing a success-metric target and treating it as a release criterion — "we will not ship until intake time is under ten minutes" — when intake time cannot even be measured until real patients, real receptionists and real clinic chaos are in the loop. A release criterion must be checkable before launch, with data available before launch. If a number can only be known after shipping, it belongs on the metrics side, full stop, however tempting it is to use it as leverage in a launch debate.

Hard gates and soft gates are a decision, not a discovery

Teams often discover, mid-review, that a criterion is "actually" soft, as Priya's team nearly did with the 95% threshold. That is a legitimate outcome only if someone with the authority to accept the residual risk says so explicitly and it gets written down; otherwise it is scope creep on safety, dressed up as pragmatism, and it erodes the next criteria list's credibility along with it.

North-star and guardrail metrics answer different questions

A north-star metric tells you whether the bet paid off; a guardrail metric tells you whether paying it off cost you something you didn't intend to spend. For Smart Intake, the north star was median walk-in-to-triage time; the guardrail was receptionist override rate, because a feature that hit its speed target only by having staff learn to ignore it would be a metric win built on a lie.

A passed gate is not a prediction of a won scoreboard

Passing every release criterion tells you the product is safe and functional; it says nothing about whether clinics will actually adopt the workflow, whether receptionists will trust the suggestions enough to act on them faster, or whether fourteen minutes was even the right baseline to beat. Confusing "cleared to ship" with "expected to succeed" is why launch teams are so often blindsided by flat success metrics after a spotless QA sign-off.

Sample size changes what a threshold means

94.2% on 500 cases and 94.2% on 50 cases are not the same claim; the smaller sample carries far more statistical noise, and a criterion written without a minimum sample size invites a team to keep testing until a lucky batch clears the bar. Jagriti's criterion specifying "at least 500 cases" was doing real work, not bureaucratic decoration.

Definitions must be frozen before the data arrives

The 94.2% versus 97.8% gap in the worked example was not a measurement error; it was two legitimate but different definitions of "correct" that had never been reconciled in writing. Any metric or criterion whose definition can still move after the result comes in is not measuring anything — it is being fitted to whatever answer the room wants that day.

Metrics cannot tell you why, only what

If Smart Intake's override rate climbs to 15% in week three, the metric will say so, but it will not say whether that is because the model got worse, because a specific clinic's patient mix is unusual, or because a new batch of receptionists was never trained. A success metric is a smoke detector, not a fire investigator; it earns its keep by prompting the right diagnostic conversation, not by having the answer built in.

Leading and lagging metrics need different launch clocks

Override rate can be read within days; whether Smart Intake actually reduced clinic staffing pressure, a lagging outcome tied to monthly rosters, cannot be read for two or three months. Reviewing both on the same 30-day cadence produces false confidence from the fast metric and false alarm from an outcome metric that was never going to move yet.

How the picture shifts by product and by company stage

Consumer products can often run release criteria and success metrics through experimentation directly on live traffic, because a mis-ranked recommendation is a bad afternoon, not a bad diagnosis. Jaivanta Play, a Bengaluru-based regional-language video streaming app, ships new recommendation-ranking changes with release criteria as light as a crash-rate ceiling and a five-percent-of-traffic exposure limit, then reads success metrics like seven-day watch time within seventy-two hours because it has millions of sessions a day to make the read statistically solid fast. Jagriti Health Cloud could not borrow that playbook even if it wanted to: a wrong triage suggestion carries clinical weight, so its release criteria had to be earned offline, on a held-out clinical sample, before a single live patient was exposed, and its success-metric read had to wait for enough real clinic-days to accumulate to be trustworthy — patience the consumer team simply did not need.

B2B products such as Jagriti's add a layer that neither consumer nor most marketplace products carry: named enterprise customers who signed contracts referencing specific behaviour, which turns some release criteria into contractual obligations rather than internal quality bars, and stretches the success-metric read across a renewal calendar rather than a usage calendar — a feature can be "succeeding" by every engagement number and still be judged a failure if it did not move the metric the clinic's owner will ask about at renewal time in October. Marketplace products carry a further complication that neither pure consumer nor pure B2B products fully share: two sides that can each pass or fail independently. Jamuna Freight Exchange, a Pune-based platform matching intercity truck loads with drivers, learned this the hard way when a change to its bidding algorithm passed every release criterion and lifted the shipper-side success metric — faster load acceptance — while quietly pushing the driver-side guardrail, average bid-to-payout gap, past its ceiling; a marketplace success-metrics document that scores only one side of the transaction is measuring half the business.

Stage matters as much as product type. An early-stage company with two hundred users can rarely wait for statistical significance before reading a success metric, and often substitutes qualitative signal — a handful of direct customer calls — for a quantitative guardrail in the first weeks, accepting more risk of being fooled by noise in exchange for speed; a large company like Jagriti at nine hundred clinics has enough volume to insist on a proper minimum-sample release criterion and a 30-day metric read with real confidence, but pays for that rigor in calendar time, which is exactly the tension Priya was navigating against her April 6 date.

Where launch reviews go wrong

The first common mistake is the one this page opened with: writing a single document that mixes gate conditions and outcome targets, so that a late-breaking metric worry gets used to relitigate a criterion that already passed, or a criterion dispute gets settled by appeal to a target that hasn't been measured yet. The symptom is a launch meeting that keeps circling back to the same slide; the underlying error is that nobody separated "may we ship" from "did it work" into two documents with two different owners and two different review moments; the cheapest diagnostic is to ask the room, out loud, which document any given objection belongs to, and refuse to proceed until someone answers.

The second mistake is defining success metrics after the data is already in, which shows up as a target that was somehow always "roughly what we hit." The underlying error is treating measurement as reporting rather than as a commitment made in advance; the fix is cheap and almost mechanical — a metrics definition document, dated and signed off before the first user sees the feature, that nobody is allowed to edit after launch day without flagging the change publicly.

The third mistake is a release-criteria list with no sample-size or measurement-window specified, which shows up as teams quietly re-running a test until it passes. The fix is to require every threshold to name its sample size or observation window in the same sentence as the number, the way Jagriti's "at least 500 cases" did — a habit cheap enough to apply to every criterion, every time.

The fourth mistake, more subtle, is a guardrail metric chosen for measurability rather than relevance — tracking something easy to instrument instead of the thing that would actually reveal harm. The symptom is a metrics dashboard that always looks fine even when frontline staff are quietly unhappy; the diagnostic is to ask a handful of the people actually using the feature, before launch, what would make them quietly stop trusting it, and check that exact behaviour is on the guardrail list.

What good looks like

Six months after Smart Intake, Jagriti shipped a second AI feature — an appointment no-show predictor — and the review looked almost unrecognisably calmer. Two documents existed from the project's second week, not its eighth: a release-criteria list with every threshold tied to a named sample size, sorted into hard and soft gates with sign-off owners next to each; and a metrics-definition document with one north-star metric (reduction in no-show rate among flagged high-risk appointments), two guardrails (false-flag rate among patients who would have shown up anyway, and receptionist time spent on the extra confirmation calls the feature triggered), and a stated 45-day read window matched to the clinics' own appointment cycle. When the go/no-go review happened, the conversation lasted twenty minutes, not two hours, because every disagreement had an obvious home — a criterion dispute went to the criteria list, a "but will it work" worry got redirected, without argument, to the metrics document and a date on the calendar when that worry would actually get an answer.

What Priya decided, and two questions to sit with

Priya did not ship on April 6 as originally scoped, and she did not slip the date either. She split the release: Smart Intake launched on schedule to the pilot clinics, but with the AI suggestion set to advisory-only for the two symptom categories responsible for the eleven genuine misroutes — chest pain and abdominal pain — routing those to a simple rules-based fallback while Arvind's team spent the following three weeks retraining specifically against that failure mode, at which point the full criterion was re-tested and cleared at 96.6%. The success-metrics document went live unchanged on April 6, instrumented from day one, so the 30-day read of walk-in-to-triage time would not lose any calendar days to the partial rollout. It was a release-criteria decision, made on release-criteria terms — narrow the scope until the gate is honestly passed — that did not touch the separate, later question of whether the feature would actually earn its keep.

The natural next stop from here is release management and launch readiness — the organisational machinery of rollback plans, staged rollouts and on-call rotations that turns a passed criteria list into a launch that survives contact with real users, which is the layer above the one this page has covered. It is also worth revisiting how the dashboard behind a success metric gets built in the first place, since a metric that cannot be reliably instrumented before launch is not a metric a team can respect thirty days later.

Two questions worth sitting with.

1. Look at the last release criterion you personally signed off on: was it checkable with data available before launch, or did it quietly borrow a number that could only be known afterward?

2. For the success metric you currently trust most, who would have to admit their idea failed if that metric came back flat — and does that person have any say over how the metric was defined?

Word count is prose only; diagrams and tables are supplementary exhibits, not filler.
