Dhanyasi Technologies: What Has To Be True To Ship

A Bengaluru collections-software firm has a release scorecard that says no, a contract that says November, and two exhibits that count different borrowers.

1. Sunday night, Indiranagar

At 11:40 pm on Sunday 18 October 2026, Ladhvika Thenappan sat with four browser tabs open and the window shut against the rain. From the lane came Bengaluru three weeks before Diwali: scooters, a generator, a rider calling a flat number up into the dark. Thenappan, Vice-President, Product at Dhanyasi Technologies Private Limited, had carried the release scorecard in her bag since Friday, as though the paper might settle if left alone.

It had not. Of the six release criteria written into the Release 12 product requirements document on 24 July, the scorecard dated Friday 16 October recorded two met and four not met (Exhibit 1). At 9:30 next morning the release committee would ask whether Dhanyasi would deploy on the night of Saturday 31 October; on Thursday 29 October, the board. Between those dates sat Annexe C of a contract signed in March 2024 with Daroob Consumer Finance LLC of Dubai, which put ₹3.31 crore of a ₹18.40 crore annual fee at risk against a success metric the PRD does not mention. The pilot had worked — she was sure of that much — and it was what she could not put down: Lakshvir Thuraisamy's one-pager and Lohanth Thillainathan's memo quoted different numbers from the same fortnight of accounts.

2. The firm, and a decision made in June 2024

Dhanyasi Technologies was founded in Chennai in 2017 by Lasyanthi Tamirisa and two colleagues out of a lending-operations team, and named after the raga her father taught. Its first product was a dunning sequencer for two-wheeler loan books: a rules engine deciding which channel to use on which day for each delinquent account. By the year to 31 March 2026 the firm, by then in Bengaluru, ran 22 lender tenants, ₹126 crore of recurring revenue and 412 people.

Daroob was won in the spring of 2024 and remains the largest single contract on the book: ₹18.40 crore a year, 14.60 per cent of FY26 recurring revenue. To hold the agreed go-live, the platform team took a decision in June 2024 that still governs what Dhanyasi can do. Rather than one feature store per region, it built a single store in Mumbai serving every tenant, isolated logically by tenant key, and minuted the physical split as work for "a later platform cycle". Tamirisa and Lavakumar Thogaru, now Director of Engineering in Pune, signed it off. It bought the date, and it is why the scorecard carries a criterion about the United Arab Emirates that cannot be cleared by writing code alone.

3. The market Dhanyasi sells into

Indian retail credit spent the four years to 2026 getting smaller per loan and far more numerous. Small-ticket unsecured lending, much of it originated at checkout behind quick-commerce apps, pushed account counts up faster than the rupees; the Reserve Bank of India's November 2023 increase in risk weights cooled pricing without reversing the count. A lender with lakhs of accounts in the 31-to-60-days-past-due bucket cannot staff a tele-calling floor against all of them, so which accounts to work, in what order, through which channel, became a software question.

The rails are shared and public: repayment mandates on NPCI's eNACH and UPI AutoPay, bureau data from TransUnion CIBIL, consented statement pulls through the Account Aggregator framework under Sahamati. So are the constraints. The RBI's digital-lending directions and fair-practice expectations bear on contact discipline — how often a borrower may be called, by whom, with what identification — and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 on what a feature store may compute and keep. Dhanyasi competes with the lending-infrastructure firms that grew up alongside it and with lenders' in-house teams, in a country whose software tradition runs through Zoho and Freshworks in Chennai. Its exposure is not only Indian: Daroob in Dubai, customer success in Singapore, design in Berlin, data science in Toronto, sales in Edison, New Jersey.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The Release 12 PRD was signed on Friday 24 July 2026. The release replaced the rules engine with a propensity ranker, which scores each account entering the 31-to-60-day bucket, orders the queue, and suppresses accounts scoring below a cut of 0.18; and it added Settle Now, a flow in which a borrower accepts a discounted settlement with no agent on the line. The PRD's metric section defined three measures: the 30-day resolution rate over accounts entering the bucket, outreach cost per resolution, and complaints per 1,000 accounts contacted. Its design section specified detection of a 1.50-point improvement at 80 per cent power, two-sided, on 14,000 accounts per arm from four tenants, allocated at account level.

On 11 August the fourth tenant, a Pune non-banking finance company, withdrew after its own audit committee declined to allocate branches mid-quarter. The pilot ran on three tenants from 18 August, and allocation went by branch cluster in onboarding order, producing arms of 9,642 and 12,815 rather than 14,000 and 14,000. Thenappan logged this on 12 August as a volume risk, but not that the design parameter had moved with it. The PRD's 1.50 points assumed account-level allocation, which carries no design effect (Exhibit 2, footnote c).

The 30-day read on the August cohort circulated on 30 September and is Exhibit 2; on Wednesday 7 October Thillainathan's memo recomputed its standard error for the branch-cluster design, moving z from 2.40 to 1.62. On 2 October a legal review of Annexe C alongside the DPDP Act had concluded that the ranker's feature computation moves Daroob borrower attributes out of the UAE. On 9 October Daroob's group chief operating officer wrote to Tamirisa confirming the figure the 24 November review would take: the 42-day resolution rate over accounts contacted at least once. On 14 October Lipunjay Thiruppathi's compliance note recorded that 2,724 of the 9,642 treatment accounts received no contact attempt in their first fourteen days, 1,942 of them because the ranker suppressed them (Exhibit 3). Exhibit 4, the money, went out with Friday's scorecard; Exhibit 5 reached her on Sunday evening.

5. The people

The decision runs through eight people in seven cities (Figure 1).

Ladhvika Thenappan — Vice-President, Product, Bengaluru
Holds that a criterion is a promise, not a target; Release 12 carries 40 per cent weight in her FY27 objectives. Not saying: she lifted RC3's attempt floor from the 2024 fair-practice checklist.
Lasyanthi Tamirisa — co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru
Has told the board Release 12 is the year's platform story; wants Daroob renewed before her Series D conversations. Not saying: she signed the June 2024 feature-store decision, and has asked legal whether Annexe C's metric can be restated without reopening the fee.

8. The options as Thenappan sees them

By Sunday evening there were four, on the back of the scorecard.

Option A — deploy on 31 October to the twenty-one tenants other than Daroob, suppression on. Daroob stays on the rules engine. RC3 is carried as a minuted exception granted by the compliance committee on 28 October, naming the borrower count, and that exception enters the January tenant audit pack. RC2, RC4 and RC5 stand, and Annexe C's 30 November production date is not met.

Option B — deploy on 31 October with the attempt floor enforced. The ranker orders the queue and suppresses nothing: the 1,942 accounts it would have suppressed are worked, and the 814 with a single attempt get a second. Priced on cohort A at the control arm's ₹19.56 per contacted account and ₹7.32 per further action, metered outreach rises from ₹68,926 to ₹1,12,869 — ₹7.15 to ₹11.71 per account entering. RC5 and the Sev-2s are untouched.

Option C — hold Release 12 and build. Stand up an inference stack inside a UAE region at ₹2.40 crore of capital expenditure plus eleven engineer-weeks at ₹1.42 lakh each, ₹15.62 lakh of loaded time; clear the Sev-2s; re-run the pilot at account level. The next deploy window after the 5–15 November freeze is Saturday 21 November, and a December cohort's first complete 42-day read closes in late January. Annexe C's remedy for missing 30 November applies: a 6 per cent fee credit, ₹1.10 crore, and a right to reopen the ₹18.40 crore fee.

Option D — amend the PRD before the 28 October committee. Replace RC3's attempt floor with an outcome criterion — no scoring decile resolving below the rules engine's rate for that decile; reset RC4 to the measured 51.42 per cent; restate the primary metric as Annexe C's 42-day rate over accounts contacted. Then deploy on 31 October. The July criteria were filed with Daroob under the March 2024 annexe, so an amendment goes to its legal team too.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The calendar is mostly not hers. The release committee meets at 9:30 on Monday 19 October. The compliance committee meets on Wednesday 28 October, its last sitting before the freeze, and is the body that can grant an exception or admit an amendment to a signed PRD. The board meets on Thursday 29 October. Deployments go out on Saturday nights, and tenants freeze changes from 5 to 15 November across the Diwali trading peak, Diwali falling on Sunday 8 November. Daroob's quarterly review is Tuesday 24 November; Annexe C's production date is Monday 30 November.

Money and people are fixed too. Daroob is ₹18.40 crore of a ₹126 crore FY26 recurring base, ₹3.31 crore of that fee at risk against the Annexe C metric. The Pune platform squad is seven engineers; between 19 October and the freeze there are thirteen working days, or 2.6 weeks, which is 18.2 engineer-weeks, 9.5 of them committed to the Sev-2 queue and the ISO audit pack. Of the 2,724 treatment accounts that received no attempt, 782 had no reachable channel on file.
